title: if and else
learningGoals: write a decision with if and else
use the colon and the indent correctly
run lines after the decision whatever the answer

youtube.title: Python if and else: Make Your Program Decide | Python Programming EP 13
youtube.description: In this episode you will write a decision with if and else, use the colon and the indent correctly and run lines after the decision whatever the answer, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Making decisions · 0:51 A two-path decision · 1:31 The path through the decision · 2:03 Second program · 3:03 Recap · 3:37 Bug of the Day · 4:25 Challenge · 4:45 Next episode

thumbnail.visual: big text "IF OR ELSE?" in tomato on peach; Xecxec standing at a fork in a beach path, one sign saying IF and the other saying ELSE; thin black border and drop shadow.
thumbnail.pose: Xecxec standing at a fork in a beach path, one sign saying IF and the other saying ELSE

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Programs become interesting when they can choose. Today we make our first real decisions with if and else.

scenes.onScreen: "Making decisions": three numbered lines (1. if checks a condition; 2. else runs when the condition is False; 3. The colon and the indent mark each block) and an analogy card: a beach lifeguard flag: red flag, you stay out; green flag, you can swim
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A decision has three parts. The word if, a condition that is True or False, and a colon. The lines indented below run only when the condition is True. Else gives the other path, for when it is False. Think of a lifeguard flag. Red flag, you stay out. Green flag, you can swim. The program checks, then walks down exactly one path.

scenes.onScreen: weather.py: a hot-day check with a block of two lines
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right; faint indent guide lines
scenes.narration: [HL 1] The temperature is thirty four. [HL 2] The condition asks, is it greater than thirty? That is True. The colon opens the block. [HL 3] First line of the block, indented. [HL 4] Second line, same indent, so it is in the same block. [HL 5] Else covers the other path. Python skips it this time. [HL 6] This line runs if the answer is False. [HL 7] The last line is at the left edge, so it runs on both paths.

code.source:
temperature = 34
if temperature > 30:
    print("Hot day")
    print("Drink water")
else:
    print("Pleasant day")
print("Enjoy the beach")
code.output:
Hot day
Drink water
Enjoy the beach

scenes.onScreen: A flowchart: condition diamond, a yes branch for the if block, a no branch for the else block, and a join before the last line
scenes.animation: Flowchart boxes light up one at a time; the arrow follows the path Python takes, and the skipped branch stays grey
scenes.narration: Here is the decision as a map. Python arrives at the diamond and asks the question. If the answer is yes, it walks the if branch. If the answer is no, it walks the else branch. Then both branches join, and the program carries on with the next line. Exactly one branch is walked every time.

scenes.onScreen: marks.py: a marks check with else
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 1] [TRACK marks=38] Marks are thirty eight. [HL 2] Is marks greater than or equal to forty? No, thirty eight is smaller. [HL 3] So the Pass line is skipped. [HL 4] Python jumps to else. [HL 5] Try again prints. Change marks to forty, and Pass prints instead. Test the edge value, forty, every time you write a condition like this.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the command types with key-tick, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as marks dot py. In the terminal, type python, space, marks dot py. Try again. Thirty eight is below the pass mark of forty.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One: if runs a block only when its condition is True. Two: else runs when the condition is False. Three: The colon opens a block and the indent shows what belongs to it. Four: A line at the left edge runs whichever path was taken. Pause the video, and say these ideas out loud, once, slowly.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: a missing colon
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We forgot the colon after the condition. Python says, syntax error, expected a colon. The arrow points to the exact spot where the colon should be. Every if line must end with a colon. It tells Python, a block starts on the next line. Add it, and the program runs.

scenes.onScreen: Why did the program stand at the fork in the road? It had many conditions to check.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: Why did the program stand at the fork in the road? It had many conditions to check.

bug.error:
Python output (exactly as Python prints it):

  File "marks.py", line 2
    if marks >= 40
                  ^
SyntaxError: expected ':'
bug.why: The colon tells Python that a block follows; without it Python cannot tell where the condition ends.

challenge: Make price = 450. Print Cheap if the price is below 500, otherwise print Expensive.
challengeAnswer: Use if price < 500: print("Cheap") and else: print("Expensive"). With 450 it prints Cheap.

shorts.title: What is if?
shorts.hook: "The if statement lets a program choose."
shorts.script: The if statement lets a program choose. You write the word if, then a condition, then a colon. The lines indented below run only when the condition is True. Think of a lifeguard flag. Green flag, you swim. Red flag, you stay out. Your program checks the condition, and then walks exactly one path. That is a decision. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Your first decision.

shorts.title: Else is the other path
shorts.script: If has a partner called else. Else runs when the condition is False. So the program always takes exactly one of the two paths, never both, never neither. Line else up under its if, put a colon after it, and indent the lines below. After both paths, the program carries on with the next line at the left edge. That line always runs. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Two paths, one runs.

shorts.title: Test the edge
shorts.hook: "Marks are thirty eight, and the pass mark is forty."
shorts.script: Marks are thirty eight, and the pass mark is forty. Is marks greater than or equal to forty? No, so Python prints Try again. Always test the edge value. At exactly forty, the condition is True, and Pass prints. The difference between greater than and greater than or equal matters. Edges are where beginner programs most often go wrong, so check them. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Test the edge value.

shorts.title: Expected a colon
shorts.script: A very common bug. You write the if line, and forget the colon at the end. Python says, syntax error, expected a colon, and the arrow points to the exact spot. The colon tells Python a block starts on the next line. Every if, else, and loop line needs one. Add the colon, and the program runs again. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Never forget the colon.

shorts.title: Pun and challenge
shorts.hook: "Why did the program stand at the fork in the road?"
shorts.script: Why did the program stand at the fork in the road? It had many conditions to check. Your challenge. Make price equal four fifty. Print Cheap if the price is below five hundred. Otherwise, print Expensive. Then try five hundred, and see what happens at the edge. Share your answer in the comments below. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 13.
shorts.caption: Try the decision.
